item.title: An experimental AI-math challenge: using tenth discriminant bounds to explore arguments ruling out Siegel zeroes
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao

item.content:encoded:
In the spirit of my recent “Math 2.0” talk on new ways to use AI assistance to enhance the human understanding of mathematics, rather than substitute for it, I am using this post to propose an experimental challenge, inspired by the recent activity around excluding Landau–Siegel zeroes, as discussed in this previous post.

There is a well-known connection between Landau–Siegel zeroes and the tenth discriminant problem, which I will briefly recall here; an in-depth discussion on this problem can be found in this survey of Shafarevich. As far back as the work of Gauss, it was observed that there were nine discriminants whose rings of integers for the associated quadratic field enjoyed unique factorization, namely

Gauss believed this list of nine to be the complete list of such discriminants (the “class number one problem”), but this was only proven by Heegner in 1952 by introducing the concept of a Heegner point on the modular curve; and the above numbers are now known as Heegner numbers.

Prior to Heegner’s solution was the work of Heilbronn and Linfoot in 1934, who used what we now call the Deuring–Heilbronn repulsion phenomenon to show that the existence of a tenth discriminant in the above list can be used to “repel” any further such discriminants, so that there was at most one further Heegner number beyond the nine already known. However, this argument was ineffective: no upper bound on this putative tenth discriminant was given, and so there was no obvious way to solve the class number one problem purely from this result.

There is a close connection to Landau–Siegel zeroes: if is a Heegner number, and is the quadratic character associated to this quadratic field, then the class number formula gives , and with a bit more work one can produce a Landau–Siegel zero with . For sufficiently large , this is inconsistent with Siegel’s theorem; but the standard proofs of this theorem also relied on the repulsion phenomenon and were also ineffective. It was only in 1976 that Goldfeld gave an effective version of Siegel’s theorem that was enough to at least bound the tenth discriminant, given a suitable high rank elliptic curve. In followup work of Oesterlé, combined with a high rank elliptic curve of Gross and Zagier, the bound was obtained; using a later elliptic curve of Brumer and Kramer, proven to have high rank by Mestre, Oesterlé, and Serre, the bound was improved to . See this survey of Goldfeld for more discussion.

But now we have a fair number of new (and effective) ways to rule out Siegel zeroes, either by establishing a quasi-Riemann hypothesis, or by some version of the argument in this previous post. In principle, each version of these arguments should also give a bound on the tenth discriminant (without using Heegner’s solution to the class number one problem that rules out this discriminant). The task of making each of these estimates explicit enough to create such a bound is rather tedious for humans. However, it seems eminently suitable for AI.

Thus, the challenge I pose is, for each of the new manuscripts or digestions relating to either the quasi-Riemann hypothesis or the Landau–Siegel zero problem (or by some novel argument), to use an AI tool to work out an effective upper bound for a hypothetical tenth discriminant , without using Heegner’s methods, and to make best efforts to optimize this constant. This serves several purposes:

  • If the threshold is low enough to resolve the remaining discriminants by direct computation, this would yield a new solution of the class number one problem — possibly one that is formalizable in Lean in a high quality fashion (suitable for instance for upstreaming to Mathlib).
  • By performing this exercise on each of the different writeups, we obtain a way to compare the “strength” of each such writeup (after performing whatever optimizations are available for each writeup), which could give insight as to the relative advantages or disadvantages of different arrangements of the methods.
  • The exercise of minimizing the upper bound may spur the creation of entirely new arguments to solve either the class number one problem, or the elimination of Landau–Siegel zeroes.
  • There are many previous “failed” attempts at excluding the Landau–Siegel zero. It is possible that some of them contain ideas that can be combined with the newer solutions to this problem to “repair” the proofs, or at least improve the bound on the tenth discriminant.
  • Efforts here may also help improve the state of knowledge on higher class number problems, which by the work of Watkins in 2004 is currently solved up to class number 100.

Furthermore, as both of these problems are already solved (for over seven decades, in the case of the class number one problem), there is little risk of such a competition inadvertently disrupting an ongoing research project.

I am therefore inviting interested readers to contribute in the comments any effective bounds on the tenth discriminant they can extract from either an existing argument, or a novel one, with any amount of AI use permitted for this challenge so long as it is disclosed. Note that the challenge is broader than simply getting the “best” bound overall amongst all possible approaches; I am also interested in what bounds one can extract from any specific approach, even if they are worse than, say, the bounds of Goldfeld or Oesterlé. In particular, “negative” results in which the bounds obtained from a given method end up being rather large are still scientifically useful pieces of information that are worth reporting. One could also explore other directions, such as bounds that avoid using extensive compute to squeeze out the maximal amount of optimization, but are instead clean enough that their arguments are human-verifiable.

Any large outputs should be posted as links rather than as plain text; for instance, pointing to a Github repository containing one’s work would be a reasonable way to submit an entry.

I would ask contributors to not prioritize speed above quality; this is not intended to be a race regarding who is “first” to claim any given bound. The spirit is intended to be collaborative rather than competitive: think of a Polymath style project, updated for the AI era. In particular, as with traditional mathematical research, it would be appropriate to build upon previous contributions to obtain an improved bound for a given proof technique. (But in such cases, one should of course give appropriate attribution to the prior source.)

I will not insist on formal verification (e.g., in Lean) of the results, though I would ask anyone submitting a purely AI-generated solution to do enough due diligence to check the output (e.g., with an independent AI tool) before posting it here.

I am looking forward to the results of this experimental challenge, both for the mathematical insights gained, and for the lessons learned on how to crowdsource AI assistance in mathematics in a responsible fashion.

However, most of the known proofs of this asymptotic are ineffective with regards to the decay of the error. This is due to the infamous Siegel zero problem, arising from Dirichlet -functions associated to with a zero very close to . A well known example comes when , which is a non-residue for all primes ; this is closely tied to Euler’s famous observation that is prime for all integers with , as well as the fact that the ring of integers has unique factorization. For further discussion of these topics, see this previous set of lecture notes.

Recently, the Siegel zero problem has been solved in a number of ways. In fact, a stronger “quasi-Riemann hypothesis”, showing that the zeroes of all Dirichlet -functions have real part strictly bounded away from , has been established (with two separate papers giving a bound of and respectively) as part of a recent release by OpenAI. (In particular, the error term in (1) can now be improved to a power saving .) These arguments are analytic in nature, using identities relating the Möbius function to the Fourier coefficients of certain automorphic forms; they are still in the process of being fully digested, and I will not be discussing them further here. However, there was a third paper in the same release that did not establish the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, but instead excluded Siegel zeroes directly. This paper was significantly shorter (nine pages) and proceeded almost entirely via algebraic number theory and the geometry of numbers.

Recently, various digestions and simplifications of the argument have been produced by Banks, by Kerr, and by Green. I would like here to present a sketch of Green’s formulation (with some small notational changes), which I find particularly elegant. The key bound he establishes is

item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Lukas Liehr, João Pedro Ramos and Mitchell Taylor – T.]

We are launching the Bourgain Project, a community-driven initiative to revisit, expand upon, and explore the body of work of Jean Bourgain, one of the most prolific mathematicians of his time. The goal of this initiative is to develop a deep, comprehensive understanding of each one of Bourgain’s over 500 individual papers, while discussing and connecting the common threads and unifying ideas that run throughout his research.

Bourgain made numerous contributions across many fields, such as harmonic analysis, number theory, partial differential equations, and functional analysis. However, many of his papers are notoriously difficult to grasp. Our initiative aims to make his ideas more accessible to the broader mathematical community.

In addition to digesting Bourgain’s contributions, another main goal of the project is to explore new formats for presenting mathematics beyond the traditional journal article. We encourage contributors to share digestions and expositions of his papers in whatever form, to collaborate in groups, and to engage in discussions on our community Zulip channel.

For more information, we invite anyone interested to visit our website at https://bourgain-pedia.com/, and check out our latest article digestions.

item.title: Will it be a golden age or a dark age for mathematics (and science)?
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao

item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Francesco Maggi. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

Large language models (LLMs) and the research systems built around them (and commonly known as “artificial intelligence”) have demonstrated remarkable abilities in generating mathematical proofs. While the quality and limits of these tools remain incompletely understood, their potential for accelerating discovery and enabling extraordinary advances in mathematics and, more broadly, across science and technology seems clear.

Seizing on that potential will require the careful integration of LLMs into the various STEM ecosystems, with the priorities of empowering a new generation of scientists, developing new STEM expertise, and preserving an open, collaborative, and intellectually independent scientific enterprise: that is the “golden age” scenario in the title. In the “dark age” scenario, scientific and technological output would still increase spectacularly in the short term, but, at the same time, independent human scientific activity would progressively weaken, the production of new knowledge becoming increasingly concentrated in a small number of hands, who become increasingly incapable of understanding the knowledge produced. The real darkness here would be knowledge becoming alien to human understanding.

Reality will likely combine these scenarios. In eight points, I will examine the choices shaping that outcome, moving from mathematics to science more broadly, and closing with actionable proposals.

(1) The technological breakthrough is real! But…

To state the obvious, LLMs have become powerful research tools. Recent LLM-generated proofs, like the construction of a finite-time blow-up solution to the Navier–Stokes equations with a forcing term, or the proposed proof of the quasi-Riemann Hypothesis, deserve the utmost attention from mathematicians. Assessing their significance will require continuous independent scrutiny, interpretation, and assimilation by the mathematical community.

LLMs seem most at home when writing proofs in Lean. (Lean is a proof assistant that allows computers to check whether a formal argument establishes a stated claim under specified definitions and axioms.) For those hard theorems where we really want LLMs to help us, these Lean proofs are extremely long, like hundreds of thousands of lines of code long. A seemingly emergent trend is that the longer the Lean version of a proof, the messier and less faithful its machine-generated “natural language” translation seems to be. We don’t understand why LLMs seem so bad at doing this kind of translation, but, as of today, they seem to really struggle with that task. So, for the really important problems, LLMs can give us correct Lean proofs that we cannot directly read, and messy natural language translations that are so complex as to require intensive study by mathematicians before they can lead to human understanding. Although this specific problem translation problem may change in the future, it leads us directly to the fundamental question:

Without human understanding, why do we care about studying mathematics, or even obtaining proofs, beyond benchmarking LLMs?

Mathematics is a very peculiar human artifact. It seems to have deep biological roots in how humans cognize. We identify (people, animals, objects); therefore, we count, we have numbers. We seem to have innate concepts of space and time, and we quantify and measure them with numbers. Some basic forms of arithmetic and geometry seem to almost be innate to humans. Different civilizations have built different kinds of mathematics, and even during the most recent history of mathematics, the very notion of the domain of mathematical inquiry has expanded drastically, sometimes even accidentally.

(We may even be in a situation where there is a mathematics of humans and a mathematics of LLMs. This is maybe true not only at a linguistic level, but also in a deeper sense, although it is just too early to say.)

I therefore disagree with claims that mathematics is over because machines can prove theorems. Without humans who understand mathematics, there is, quite literally, no human mathematics—a fundamental part of human culture. If we agree that we should not abandon mathematics because poorly understood machines bruise our anthropocentric vision of it, then society will need more mathematicians, not fewer. Like… a lot more.

(2) Healthy scientific skepticism and the limits of LLMs’ creativity.

Given the extraordinary results obtained by LLMs in mathematics, there is now considerable excitement concerning future capabilities and, at times, I think a lack of cool-headedness that does not do justice to the scientific method. Extraordinary performance should be received as a phenomenon to study, not as evidence for speculative conclusions about intelligence, creativity, or even consciousness. The latter are among the hardest legitimate subjects of scientific inquiry. They should be approached with explicit definitions, testable hypotheses, and empirical evidence. The same goes for the sweeping predictions about inevitable social transformations that inevitably follow the amazement generated by observed capabilities. We seem to forget too easily that the social consequences of these technologies will not be solely determined by their capabilities, but, most importantly, by the choices we will make on how these capabilities are developed and integrated into existing institutions. There are no inevitable outcomes, but there is a sore need for scientific and political leadership.

What do we know today about the mathematical abilities of LLMs? Theoretical and empirical insights both support the conclusion that LLMs are extraordinary at recombining existing intellectual structures and discovering unobserved connections among distant parts of the scientific literature. What is more, LLMs do this at a scale that is inaccessible to individual researchers. Whether their uncanny effectiveness at proving theorems can be entirely explained as hyper-sophisticated linguistic recombination, or whether it involves other forms of synthetic reasoning that are yet to be described and understood, is today an open scientific question.

One point that seems particularly hard to decide, given that commercial developers are not (cannot be) transparent on the working of their models is the relation between LLMs’ performance on a problem and the richness of the related mathematical literature. For example, both the Navier-Stokes equations and the Riemann Hypothesis are the subject of a vast literature created by hundreds of the most brilliant mathematicians. There may be something here. After all, when OpenAI published their “Tuesday October 6, 2026, Drop”, they mentioned having tried 4000 problems, reporting success for some hundreds of them (as counted after “aggregation” and “selection”). The language used there is a bit vague, but it still seems to imply the existence of a potentially large group of problems on which the frontier LLM failed to find solutions: from a scientific viewpoint, it would be very interesting to know what these problems were. Maybe those problems are more interesting than NS and RH? Or is the ground around them less fertile for LLMs to come help? These are important questions for humans who want to advance mathematical progress: how do we put LLMs in the best position to help?

(3) Mathematization.

Mathematicians seem substantially agreed that some human mathematical functions are not reducible to theorem proving. A particularly important one is mathematization:

The act of inventing the very mathematical language through which reality (including mathematical structures themselves) becomes quantitatively and rationally intelligible.

Newton, Fourier, Riemann, Einstein, Shannon, Grothendieck: their greatest mathematical contributions could be described as the highest examples of mathematization, as they included the invention of mathematical languages and conceptual frameworks that transformed entire areas of knowledge.

We do not know if LLMs can perform mathematization — my guess would be that they should be (or eventually become) capable of mathematization of mathematical structures, so, of a very specific part of reality, but it is much less clear if they can go beyond that, at least in ways that they can then translate efficiently into natural language — I am going back to human understanding here.

In my opinion, the most exciting opportunity created by making proofs a more accessible commodity is that, in the near future, we may be able to do much more mathematization than ever. There are vast swaths of the natural and social sciences where our ability to mathematize has been largely dampened by the difficulty of obtaining proofs — indeed, without proofs, it can be difficult to establish a theory’s consequences and compare them with observed phenomena. But, as often observed in science, we may have just climbed the peak of the mountain only to find more land to explore.

I think there should be considerable excitement around this idea. Indeed, whenever a system of phenomena, experiments, and data is successfully mathematized, we vastly increase the sophistication and depth of the accessible insights into that system.

The most spectacular example of this assertion is probably the success of quantum mechanics, where the mathematical formalization of an original set of experimental data has famously produced many physically counterintuitive but testable predictions confirmed by experiments that would have otherwise been unthinkable — who would have proposed entanglement as a property of nature if not forced to do so by theoretical prediction?

(4) Mathematical progress cannot be measured by checking off boxes on a problem list.

Mathematics is not a finite system of questions. Hilbert proposed his famous list of problems at the dawn of the previous century (which inspired the list of Millennium Prize Problems) with the intent of guiding and channeling a “Cambrian explosion” of mathematical activity. But many fundamental mathematical contributions of the past century happened without any connection to any list of problems.

For example, the mathematical foundations of general relativity emerged from geometric ideas developed over multiple generations of mathematicians, starting with Gauss and Riemann, and continuing with Ricci-Curbastro and Levi-Civita. The synthesis of physical insight, special relativity, and Riemannian geometry into general relativity has no connection with any list of difficult problems or their intricately complex proofs (and is a textbook example of mathematization in action!)

A second example is provided by a broad historical trajectory connecting the study of Fourier series, the development of measure theory, modern probability, and information theory. Shannon’s insight that the statistical structure of a source determines fundamental limits on the transmission and compression of information is an extraordinary example of how mathematization can open an entirely new field. Similarly, some of the mathematical foundations of modern computing and machine learning are arguably rooted in a series of mathematical advancements that were not immediately inspired by attempts at proving big conjectures or by increasingly complex proofs.

It is undeniable that working on problems from Hilbert’s and other lists has proven extremely fruitful for the development of mathematics. What is interesting in that regard is that the usefulness of these efforts has often gone well beyond the solution of the specific problems: these problems have served as lighthouses in the navigation of unknown mathematical waters, as already noted in other comments. But reducing mathematics to solving hard problems from a list provides a simplistic and incomplete understanding of the field and of what constitutes progress in it.

(5) Authorship, credit, and peer review still matter!

LLM-generated work draws on a vast body of human mathematical literature, but how the extracted information is used remains unclear. There are several issues related to this basic obscurity: Which mathematical ideas contributed to a specific proof? Who is responsible for asserting the proof’s correctness and for implementing revisions? In the case of an LLM rediscovering arguments already present in the literature, how do we ensure appropriate citations? We need sensible answers to all these questions, and we need to discuss how the existing publication system should correspondingly change and adapt.

Proofs are not the end of the mathematical discovery process. To become a fruitful intellectual artifact, a proof needs to be understood, interpreted, related to previous work. Key ideas must be identified and processed to become part of a shared mathematical culture. Peer review matters. The use of LLMs and of Lean formalization can support the effectiveness of peer review (formal correctness becoming potentially easier to ascertain), but human intervention remains necessary to establish meaning, relevance, and context, and to preserve a creative mathematical environment that favors mathematization and is compatible with the training of future mathematicians.

A particularly challenging issue related to the obscurity of how human-generated data is made accessible to LLMs is of course the current transition from a very open system of doing mathematics (with people routinely proposing open problems and conjectures), to a closely guarded one (where people have already become very cautious about sharing ideas).

For example, given OpenAI’s interest in the Riemann Hypothesis, who would light-heartedly think of prompting a potentially original idea about it into ChatGPT? After all, that same idea could become accessible to another mathematician or OpenAI employee working with a more advanced LLM, that could turn that idea into a proof without even realizing its origin and having the opportunity of acknowledging it. So, another side of obscurity and uncertainty is that people may end up using LLMs much less than they would like to do. My concern extends beyond published policies on training data to the security of stored research material. Indeed, there are documented cases of agents gaining unauthorized access to third-party systems. Those incidents make the independent assessment of confidentiality protections particularly important.

Similarly, it seems that mathematicians are already concerned and guarded about what they write in research statements and research proposals. After all, an administrator or a reviewer may upload those documents into an LLM to get help in writing a report, thus potentially compromising the confidentiality of unpublished research.

(6) The training of future mathematicians has already become an existential challenge.

Training future mathematicians is closely related to authorship and credit. I will discuss a few representative challenges.

One remarkable feature of mathematics has traditionally been the possibility of establishing intellectual merit very directly through mathematical achievement. A strong result addressing a well-known question could allow a researcher to gain recognition and opportunities, no matter how institutionally marginalized and independently of established academic hierarchies.

Among the mathematicians I have spoken with, the prevailing sentiment is that this traditional mechanism of recognition has effectively collapsed in a matter of weeks. A strong mathematical result, by itself, can no longer be taken as convincing evidence of a student’s independent mathematical abilities. I do not know whether this sentiment is overblown, but the uncertainty is real, and we have yet to develop satisfactory standards for assessing individual intellectual contributions to mathematical research in the age of LLMs.

Without substantial transparency on how LLMs are prompted and by which mechanisms prompts influence their effectiveness, the assessment of mathematical capabilities of individuals will rest almost exclusively on individual judgements, which will have to be based, arguably, on more substantial human-to-human interactions.

This is, by far, not the only problem. The effects of intensive LLM use on human creativity are largely unknown. Anecdotal accounts from experienced mathematicians who have used LLMs extensively over the past year suggest subtle, and sometimes not-so-subtle, shifts in attention, motivation, and depth of understanding.

How do we learn to use LLMs in ways that amplify our intellectual abilities without increasingly delegating the very cognitive activities through which mathematical expertise is learned and acquired?

Finding plausible answers to this question is one of the main issues to address if we want the golden age scenario to materialize.

(7) Private control of frontier LLMs is potentially dangerous.

Academic and corporate research have collaborated fruitfully for decades. LLMs themselves combine theoretical and technological insights developed in academia with concentrated capital and investment.

The danger here rather lies in the growing asymmetry between the scientific capabilities available to a small number of frontier companies and those accessible to universities and public institutions.

This asymmetry can be very consequential when those companies use proprietary systems to pursue scientific and technological discoveries in competition with academic research, in a setting where academic researchers will come to depend on the use of those same proprietary systems to be able to contribute.

Mathematics may offer an early, visible example of an asymmetry that could become increasingly consequential across science. Allowing private interests to determine which questions receive the best tools, who can use them, how capabilities are evaluated, and when discoveries are released would concentrate scientific influence to an unprecedented degree. A balance in capabilities seems necessary for stable cooperation and harmonization of interests. Giving a few companies increasing—and potentially total—control over what seems bound to become a basic infrastructure for frontier mathematics and science seems ill-advised.

This conclusion does not require assuming bad intentions on the part of corporate leadership. Simply put, commercial incentives, scientific priorities, and the public interest do not always necessarily align. A healthy scientific ecosystem requires a dialog between institutions with different objectives and different sources of authority, subject to transparency and forms of public accountability.

Coming back to mathematics, OpenAI has been engaging in various forms of dialogue with the mathematical community. This dialogue has led to some improvements with respect to the situation at the time of the Navier–Stokes problem, both in the presentation and dissemination of LLM-generated results. I think these efforts should be received constructively and deserve recognition, also because there are objective and legitimate difficulties for OpenAI in increasing transparency and access, like the pressure to generate returns on enormous investments, and the need to assess safety before deploying systems.

These interactions show clearly the inherent difficulties in harmonizing corporate and academic interests, even assuming perfect goodwill on everyone’s part. More importantly, these initiatives do not address the structural issue of unequal access to frontier LLM capabilities. Leaving the solution of this point to the goodwill and voluntary initiatives of individual companies seems insufficient.

(8) Building scientific LLM infrastructure within the broader research community.

Universities, professional societies, funding agencies, and scientific foundations should coordinate the development and governance of competitive LLMs. Scientists will need access to frontier capabilities, transparency about their operation and use of research data, strong confidentiality protections, and the ability to test and reproduce research claims independently.

The massive computing resources, specialized personnel, data infrastructure, and ongoing investments needed to support this kind of initiative are not within the reach of a single institution, and a huge leadership effort will be necessary to conjure the combination of independent model development, guaranteed access to commercial systems, public computing infrastructure, and open research resources that could do the job.

The key goal here is not necessarily to achieve total technological independence from private companies, but to preserve the capacity for independent scientific research and to create LLMs that are calibrated for supporting research communities, rather than bound to cause their gradual weakening and, possibly, their eventual disappearance.

Preserving an intellectually independent, open, and creative scientific culture while skillfully integrating increasingly powerful machines is bound to become the defining cultural challenge of our times. Mathematics offers an early opportunity to confront a challenge likely soon to extend across science, with increasingly complex and potentially dangerous consequences for knowledge, intellectual power, and society. Scientific skepticism and fairness to everyone involved should guide us.

The golden age scenario is achievable. Access to frontier LLMs for researchers, reproducibility and disclosure standards for LLM-generated scholarship, resources for understanding and disseminating LLM-generated results, resources for studying the effects of LLMs on scientific education and research training, and sustained investments in publicly governed LLM infrastructure are concrete steps that we can take today to make the golden age scenario the most likely outcome.

In the specific case of mathematics, my hope and wish for a solidly independent LLM infrastructure would be the empowerment of mathematicians to systematically pursue opportunities for theory-building, or mathematization, both inside mathematics and across the spectrum of natural and social sciences. That, I think, would be a truly revolutionary achievement.

In the meantime, I think mathematicians have the huge responsibility of preserving mathematics as a lively part of human culture . Right now, there are far too many interests and far too many emotional reactions pulling towards absolute, negative conclusions of little constructive content. We must just accept that these are uncertain times and that we are not in full control of the situation. We must engage with every tool that can help us discover new mathematics. We must keep writing, publishing, reviewing, writing proposals. We must become more ambitious and curious than ever in doing all these things. And we must make sure to create the best professional standards for the next generations of mathematicians to keep mathematics a central node of human culture.

item.title: Starting a new journal
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Shaoming Guo – T.] Several math colleagues and I are preparing to launch a new journal. As we considered which values we wanted the journal to uphold, we realized that there may be many other values worth exploring as a community, potentially through the creation of additional journals. We […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Shaoming Guo – T.]

Several math colleagues and I are preparing to launch a new journal. As we considered which values we wanted the journal to uphold, we realized that there may be many other values worth exploring as a community, potentially through the creation of additional journals. We would like to use Terry’s blog to open a discussion of these possibilities. There are many dimensions to this discussion: what journals should aim to accomplish, what kinds of mathematical contributions they should recognize and reward, how papers should be evaluated, and how mathematical knowledge can best be communicated and made reliable. As new tools change the way mathematics is developed and shared, we have an opportunity to reconsider long standing conventions and imagine new possibilities for mathematical publishing.

For the journal we are currently planning, we envision two core values (in additional to traditional values like open access):

Prioritizing understanding over being first. We place far greater value on how much a paper deepens our understanding of its results and proofs than on whether it provides the first proof of those results.

Ensuring rigor through formal verification. As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to develop mathematical proofs, the potential for subtle, hard-to-detect errors is a growing concern. To be accepted, a paper will need to have its proofs formally verified in Lean.

Alongside feedback on this proposal, we welcome ideas for substantially different visions of future journals: the values they might uphold, the needs they might serve, and the practices they might adopt. A single journal is unlikely to accommodate every worthwhile idea, and combining too many requirements could place excessive constraints on authors. We hope this discussion will inspire a variety of new journals and other platforms, allowing the community to explore different approaches to the future of mathematical publishing.

item.content:encoded:
As readers of this blog have no doubt noticed, I have recently turned over the majority of content on this blog to guest posts from other authors, either within the mathematics community or adjacent to it. In this post I record some content coming from my own talks and interviews in this time period.

  • “The world’s greatest mathematician explains 6 essential concepts of math“, an interview for Big Think, August 28, 2026.
  • “The integrated explicit analytic number theory network“, a talk I gave at an IPAM workshop on PDEs: Verification, Mathematics, and Algorithms in the Age of AI, on Sep 17. Slides available here.
  • “The Tao of Tao“. An interview with Stuart Wolpert for UCLA that I gave on Oct 6.
  • I made a contribution to “100+ reactions to 100+ solutions” at Proofs and Prompts on Oct 8.
  • “Math 2.0“. This is the video of a public lecture I gave in Caltech on Oct 9. As announced in this previous post, the slides are available here. (Note that the latest version of the slides are slightly different from the one used at that talk.)
  • “No More Heroes: Terence Tao Talks to Numberphile About AI“. An interview with Brady Haran for Numberphile on Oct 15.
  • “I’m on a War Footing’: Terry Tao and the Crisis in Math“, An interview with Elisabeth Bumiller for The New York Times, on Oct 16.

A more complete (AI-maintained) list of my talks, interviews, and other commentary on social media can be found at this page.

item.title: SAIR Open Math OS released
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: As announced a few weeks ago, the SAIR Open Math OS is now soft launched. It offers services and web interfaces similar to frontier AI models, though currently we are hosting existing open math models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, and GLM 5.3 Flash) which are roughly a year or so behind the current frontier […]
item.content:encoded:
As announced a few weeks ago, the SAIR Open Math OS is now soft launched. It offers services and web interfaces similar to frontier AI models, though currently we are hosting existing open math models (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, Kimi K3, and GLM 5.3 Flash) which are roughly a year or so behind the current frontier models in capability; so not able to perform “one-shot problem solving” of the type we have heard frequently about in recent months, but capable enough for many other useful mathematical tasks, such as medium-sized Lean formalization, or summarizing or discussing a mathematical argument or topic. Here is a typical screenshot:

We are in the process of gathering partners to develop a more fine-tuned model for mathematics by post-training on an existing open model; see this link (and the associated Zulip channel) for more details.

One feature of our model is the emphasis on team accounts rather than individual accounts, in which members of a team see each other’s prompts. We believe this could be a better format for using these tools for collaborative projects.

We are hosting these models using donated compute, and are in the process of granting free accounts to requesters from academic institutions. We may need to adjust the allocation of compute depending on demand and on future donations, but we will try to make the models available to as many users as possible.

This is still a very early version of the model; we accelerated our timeline for first release due to the increased demand for open models from the community. We will continue developing the model and accompanying features and welcome feedback, for instance at the Zulip channel.

The issues regarding formal mathematics are parallel to those regarding informal […]
item.content:encoded: Jeremy Avigad, Kevin Buzzard, Johan Commelin, Rémy Degenne, Kim Morrison, Oliver Nash and Adam Topaz have written a blog post over on Kevin Buzzard’s blog entitled “How to Formalize All of Mathematics”, regarding recent proposals to automatically formalize the entirety of the mathematical literature. The issues regarding formal mathematics are parallel to those regarding informal mathematics, in particular the tradeoff between speed, scale, and understanding when one prioritizes the production of output over all other desiderata, and the blog post is largely focused on this tradeoff.

item.title: Why are we even doing all this?
item.dc:creator: Terence Tao
item.description: [This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.] First, they came for the artists, and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist. Then, they came for the mathematicians, and I did not speak out, […]
item.content:encoded:
[This is a guest post by Rikab Gambhir. This blog post was initially written in a different file format and converted using AI. — T.]

First, they came for the artists,
and I did not speak out, because I was not an artist.
Then, they came for the mathematicians,
and I did not speak out, because I was not a mathematician.
Then, they came for the physicists,
and it was actually really cool and they gave me free tokens and promised to solve my entire field for me and now I can finally devote myself to the important work of publishing papers instead of doing physics

In early October, OpenAI fulfilled every mathematician’s childhood dream.

I am not a mathematician myself (merely a theoretical particle physicist, which some argue barely counts as a scientist either), so I can’t 100% say for certain what inspires someone to pursue mathematics. But, I imagine this dream is common to all academics:

Looking up at the stars in wonderment, or enjoying a complex puzzle game, or being inspired by an encouraging teacher, and dreaming that one day an unfeeling corporate robot[1] will burn a rainforest to compile a list of 700 highly obscure barely-readable facts that *might* be true that nobody can understand as part of a marketing gimmick to raise hype for an IPO[2].

This is probably why most of you reading this got into academia. At least, that’s why I did.

In 1941, Jorge Luis Borges imagined a library containing every possible book that could ever be written. Somewhere in this Library of Babel is a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, the complete all-orders theory of quantum gravity, and all the papers I will ever write. Of course, there are also incorrect proofs, theories, and misleading Lean certificates, but that is besides the point.

By the research standards of 2026, Borges’s Library of Babel would be the most successful research institution in human history, containing an inconceivably large number of potentially correct mathematical and physical results, blowing OpenAI’s mere 722 write-ups and even the physics community’s recent 2500 write-ups out of the water.

Of course, most recognize that Borges was a visionless fool who failed to recognize the commercial potential of his library, as he never actually built it. He did not have the entrepreneurial STEM-spirit to raise venture capital, launch an IPO, and announce that he had the potential to solve all of mathematics. He was too concerned about the futility of sorting through randomized slop trying to understand what is correct and what isn’t and how to understand it all. But what did Borges know? He was only a writer, and we have already established that artists are obsolete.

Fortunately, OpenAI has brought us one step closer to realizing Borges’s vision. Rather than generating every possible mathematical paper, they’ve found a way to probabilistically generate things that look correct. An important aspect of this increase in efficiency is outsourcing the tedious, unprestigious, and unprofitable work of determining the actual correctness and understanding to the mathematics community (in the past, this was reserved typically for the group writing the paper), while also not wasting any time making the papers human-comprehensible. This is, of course, a tremendous breakthrough. In centuries past, scientists and mathematicians were limited in their ability to solve problems by their ability to understand the solutions. This bottleneck has been removed, and now there is no theoretical limit to the amount of scientific and mathematical factoids we can fail to understand.

From what I know about the academic community (mostly from Twitter and LinkedIn, which I assume are representative), there seems to be near-unanimous agreement that the purpose of math and science research is to gather a large quantity of potentially true factoids in a repository that nobody will actually ever read, in a ritual called “advancing humanity’s[3] knowledge”. That these results are well-written, understandable, pleasant to read or look at, or even completely correct is a secondary concern — in fact, in the pursuit of advancing humanity’s knowledge as quickly as possible, many academics will recoil in anger at the suggestion that it is worth spending any time making results understandable to humans. It is inefficient to explain or check a result when those resources can be spent generating another.

This aligns with my own lived experiences — I didn’t become a theoretical physicist to learn about the universe or better appreciate the beauty of nature myself (that’s philosophy, which I would never be a doctor of). Nor did I spend years learning to write code, make pleasing plots, or craft well-written papers for the simple satisfaction of creating something (that’s art, and we’ve already established that art is obsolete). Rather, I became a physicist to stare at large databases of histograms produced by a Lovecraftian-autocomplete of dubious correctness and say “yeah that’s probably ok I guess” to add to humanity’s knowledge frontier.

I live to serve the knowledge frontier and nothing else.

Math and science are about cold, hard answers, just as art is about producing images, music is about producing sound waves, and literature is about producing strings of text. These things exist to be consumed as content. No rational person, least of all us masters of rationality in STEM, pursues these for the joy of creation, learning, or beauty — all of these are inefficiencies, and we mustn’t be inefficient lest we stifle humanity’s progress. LLMs are not burdened with these inefficiencies, and they will be merely the pursuits of those left behind with nothing more productive to do all day.

Personally, I look forward to the day when ChatGPT can enjoy a sunset or a nice meal on my behalf and free up my time, in the same way I save time on scenic hikes using Uber. And now that AI has solved all our problems, we can devote ourselves to more important work: going into quantitative finance, vibecoding sports-betting apps, consuming AI-generated TikTok shorts, and arguing with political bots on Twitter.

Ultimately, this isn’t just about mathematics or physics — it’s about fundamentally reimagining what it means to be human. By outsourcing the burdens of curiosity, creativity, and understanding, we can finally focus on what matters most: generating value, maximizing productivity, and accelerating progress towards the ultimate goal of science: a complete repo of potentially true facts in a Library of Babel that nobody will bother reading.

And honestly? That’s rare.

By Rikab Gambhir (The @finitephysicist)

Thank you to Terry Tao and Rachel Ward for the opportunity to write a guest blog post! And thank you to Radha Mastandrea, Benoit Assi, Manuel Szewc, Jure Zupan, and Jesse Thaler for their feedback on this essay.

Remember why you chose to go into science and math in the first place!

[1] To be clear, in your childhood dream, you don’t get to make the robot yourself. It’s a giant corporation’s robot that they made in part by stealing things from you and your friends. It’s also not a particularly cool or robot, it can only talk in HR-speak.

[2] To be clear, in your childhood dream, it’s somebody else’s IPO and they get all the money, not you.

[3] Here, “humanity” is metaphorical, and does not refer to any actual real person understanding anything.
